column41: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the family Commelinaceae; herbaceous monocot with conspicuous flowers in parts of 3 (6 tepals in 2 whorls of 3), a superior ovary and parallel veins in leaves. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the genus Tradescantia; multiple pedicellate flower clusters enclosed with 2 large leafy bracts. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Tradescantia fluminensis; the dark green top surface of the leaves, the lighter green underside of the leaves, 3 free white inner tepals, 3 green outer tepals, 6 yellow anthers on filaments tufted with white hairs and no occurrence of fruit. It is unlikely to be the species Tradescantia zebrina which has pink tepals and purple on the underside of its leaves. Extra info: While amazing for groundcover, this plant is not ideal for native species conservation. The competitiveness of this plant has been incredibly damaging to our native habitats and plants. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

column41: I have depicted this flower as a part of the Iridaceae family due to the fact that it contains 2 different types of petals which is a common aspect of the Iridaceae family. The three outer petals have a yellow strip in the middle which is only present on half of the petal. Whereas, the inner petal is mostly white with aspects of yellow towards the base. There is also 3 purple, petal like structures at the center of the flower which matches the description of the genus Dietes. The flower is radially symmetrical and also contains an inferior ovary. It forms a bush like structure, where the length of the stem is quite long and clean as it ends in 1 or more fortnight lily flowers. The leaves are a long thin strip like structure with a pointed end. It is connected from the base of the plant and contains parallel veins indicating it is a monocot plant type. The dead flowers form a hard shell like structure where there petal like structures which is hollow on the inside.

column41: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the Myrtaceae family; woody shrub, simple entire leaves with oil glands, actinomorphic flowers with 5 petals, a half inferior ovary and numerous showy stamens. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the Genus Kunzea; dehiscent fruit, flower buds without calyptras, free stamens that exceed petals in length, alternate leaves, thin leaves (<5mm wide), persistent sepals and flowers on leaf axils. Although Genus Kunzea and Leptospermum appear similar, the filaments of Kunzea exceed petal length unlike Leptospermum (filaments shorter than petals), hence why the plant is Genus Kunzea. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Kunzea ambigua; white flowers crowded near leaves, short pedicels and villous young stems. While Kunzea axillaris and Kunzea occidentalis are similar to K. ambigua, K. axillaris has far shorter leaves (3-5mm compared to 4-12mm) and K. occidentalis has more glabrous young stems. Extra Info: K. ambigua has a distinctly strong and enjoyable smell. Also, Les Robinson speculates that the term "ambigua" (meaning doubt in Latin) indicates the founders' original confusion with this species regarding its classification as Kunzea or Leptospermum. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

column41: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the family Solanaceae; woody shrub, purple flowers with 5 petals and berries as fruit. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the genus Solanum; pinnatisect leaves, firm berries and stellate, purple, 5 lobed flowers in a cymose/panicle-like inflorescence (Fig 5). Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Solanum aviculare; non-climbing, erect, light violet corolla, entire margins with leaf length at 2-8 times as its width, leaves are either lobed or entire with a stalk, egg-shaped berries and mostly glabrous on all surfaces. This species is commonly confused with Solanum laciniatum. However, the above pictures show no notches in the corolla lobes. It is also confused with Solanum vescum which unlike S. aviculare has a spherical shaped berry and stalkless leaves. Unfortunately, the berries aren’t ripe, and the final colour isn’t known to be able to effectively use the key. Hence the focus is on the berries shape and leaves. Extra info: The common name, Kangaroo apple is inspired by the shape of the leaves which is thought to resemble a kangaroo’s foot. Whilst the scientific name ‘aviculare’ refers to little bird in Latin after the wing-like appendages on the leaves. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

column41: Clade: Monocots Family: Asparagaceae Genus: Lomandra Species: Lomandra hystrix (green mat-rush) - This species is in the Asparagaceae family as it is a shrub. Another trait which identifies this species in the Asparagaceae family is that it has long, hairless leaves with parallel venation. - This species is in the genus Lomandra as it contains long and narrow leaves which resemble blades. Furthermore, the base of the plant does not contain a stem. - Another feature which places this species in the Asparagaceae family is the fact that its flowers are arranged in whorled inflorescences. - Each inflorescence contains a cluster of spiky bracts. The flowers are very small and either white or cream coloured. - Lomandra hystrix is very similar to Lomandra longifolia, though I have excluded this possibility through the fact that the leaves of this species is pointed at the end, whereas the leaves of Lomandra longifolia end in a ‘W’ shape. - Yet another feature which distinguishes this species from L.longifolia is the fact that its flowers are in branched inflorescences (which are also open and loose), whereas the flowers of L.longifolia are not branched (as observed on Plantnet)

column41: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the Fabaceae family; woody shrub, legumes as fruit and flowers with 5 free petals. This plant is of the Fabaceae subfamily, Caesalpinioideae as the flowers are irregular with a non-papilionaceous corolla and equally sized petals. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the Genus Senna; absent spines/prickles, pinnately compound leaves, yellow petals and flat dehiscent pods. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Senna didymobotrya; 7-15 leaflet pairs per leaf, absent glands on leaves, tall raceme inflorescence with dark brown bracts, 2 conspicuous anthers and oblong pods with depressions between the seeds. All other Senna species do not have as tall of a raceme and have much lighter coloured bracts. Extra info: This plant is commonly referred to as the popcorn plant as rubbing the leaves will bring about the scent of buttered popcorn, however, it does depend on the person. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

column41: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the family Pteridaceae; sorus (spore-producing organs) on the underside protected by recurved margin (false indusium), highly divided lamina with compound fronds, and no flowers nor seeds. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the genus Pteris; linear, a submarginal sori covered by false indusium, a discontinuous sori in narrow bands, pinnately compound fronds with glabrous lamina and was not growing in a brackish environment. Thirdly, it is the species Pteris tremula due to the following qualities; a discontinuous linear sorus (doesn’t extend between segments nor along the apices of each pinnule/pinna), pale green tripinnate fronds, brown rachis, narrow extensions of frond apices and a deep groove running through the middle of the fronds. There may be confusion with the other two tripinnate Pteris species, Pteris comans and Pteris microptera. The above species have dark green fronds and yellowish rachis, making our current species easy to identify just by colour. Extra info: The Latin word ‘tremula’ means trembling. Also, the fronds of this species can grow up to 2m in length. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

column41: This species is the Hibbertia scandens, from the Dilleniaceae family and Hibbertia genus. Dilleniaceae consists of species with alternate, simple and entire leaves. Its flowers are actinomorphic and mostly yellow, with 5 sepals and 5 petals. The genus Hibbertia contains flowers with stamens that are numerous and free - its filaments are not united into a tube. The species Hibbertia scandens is a climbing species with long stems. Its leaves are obovate, simple, base tapering and are arranged alternately along the stem. Its leaf margins are entire. Its flowers are yellow, with numerous stamens surrounding few carpels.

column41: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the Euphorbiaceae family; woody shrub with alternate leaves and fruit within a schizocarpic 3 chambered ball. Unfortunately, there were no flowers at the time. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the Genus Ricinus; encapsulated fruit with caruncles, wide peltate leaves with toothed margins and is 7-9 palmately lobed. Thirdly, it is the species Ricinus communis as it is the only species of the genus Ricinus in the world. Otherwise, the red caruncles, green fruit and absent stipules are also features of R. communis. Extra info: The product castor oil is derived from the seeds of this plant. However, these seeds also contain a toxin called ricin, therefore raw seeds should ideally not be consumed. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET.
